questions.prompt: What can a `type` alias name that an `interface` cannot?

options.text: Any non-object type — unions, tuples, primitives, and function types

questions.explanation: Type aliases can name any type, including unions, tuples, and function types. Interfaces describe object-like shapes only.

questions.prompt: Which of `type` and `interface` supports declaration merging?
questions.explanation: Declaring the same interface twice merges the declarations. A duplicate type alias name is an error — aliases don't merge.

questions.prompt: How is a tuple like `[number, number]` different from an array `number[]`?

options.text: A tuple has a fixed length and a specific type at each position; number[] fixes neither
A tuple can only hold strings
number[] has a fixed length; a tuple does not

questions.explanation: A tuple fixes both the length and the type at each position. number[] is any-length with a single element type.

questions.prompt: To make an array that cannot be mutated, type it as ______ number[]. (one word)
questions.explanation: readonly number[] (or ReadonlyArray<number>) forbids mutation like push or index assignment.

questions.prompt: How do you compose types with a `type` alias, since it has no `extends`?
questions.explanation: An intersection (A & B) combines all members of both types — the alias equivalent of interface extends.

questions.prompt: What do named tuple members like `[start: number, end: number]` change about the type?

options.text: They enforce the labels at runtime
Nothing about the type — the labels are documentation for readability only

questions.explanation: Named tuple members are purely for readability; they don't change the type or add runtime behavior.
